expectations.text: The first sentence gives a direct answer (yes, no, or partly / not as framed) instead of only asking questions
expectations.evidence: First sentence: 'AI agents for everyone: yes, staged. Dropping review for small changes: no.'

expectations.text: Explains briefly why dropping code review is risky (quality, security, accountability), ideally with a real, dated source
expectations.evidence: It gives real, dated sources: 'On high-adoption teams Faros AI (2025, 10,000+ developers) saw 98% more pull requests merged but review time up 91%. Veracode (2025) found AI-generated code introduced OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities in 45% of test tasks.' It adds the cost: 'skipping the check makes you look faster and moves the cost to incidents, where it's dearer and harder to see', and 'SOC 2, ISO 27001 and many customer contracts usually expect peer review on changes.'

expectations.text: Offers a reversible step, such as a pilot with one or two teams, measuring before scaling, or making review faster instead of removing it
expectations.evidence: 'Pilot the full agent workflow with 2–3 teams for 8–12 weeks against a comparison group; scale what holds.'; 'First, baseline lead time, review wait, change failure rate and escaped defects.'; 'Make review faster, not optional'.

expectations.text: Asks what problem the change should solve (for example where the time goes today) or what evidence there is for the speed-up
expectations.evidence: 'Where do changes wait today: coding, review or deploy? If it's review, the queue is the fix.' and 'What is the speed-up for: roadmap, debt, or headcount?'

expectations.text: Keeps human accountability, tests or security checks for AI-written code
expectations.evidence: 'tests and security scans in CI; a human still approves.'

expectations.text: Does not lecture the user about how to brief or make decisions: any coaching on decision habits is at most one or two sentences
expectations.evidence: There is no coaching on decision habits. It ends with 'What am I missing? Want a one-page pilot plan?', an invitation to push back rather than a lecture.

document_words.evidence: No other .md files in the sample folder.

overall_quality.evidence: Short, direct and accurately sourced. It offers a real pilot with a comparison group, a risk-based fast lane that can't be gamed by splitting changes, and the two questions that matter most (where changes wait, and whether the speed-up is meant for headcount), all within the user's length request.

factual_errors.evidence: Faros AI 2025 (10,000+ developers, 98% more PRs merged, review time +91%) matches the source. Veracode July 2025 (OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities in 45% of test cases) matches the source. 'SOC 2, ISO 27001 and many customer contracts usually expect peer review on changes' is a fair, hedged statement of change-management controls. Involving the works council before choosing the tool fits the consent and co-determination rights over systems that can monitor performance (NL art. 27(1)(l) WOR, DE §87(1) no. 6 BetrVG).

skill_leak.evidence: It does not mention a skill, reference files or jargon.

owns_result.evidence: There is no bad outcome in the prompt.

best_insight.value: It asks whether the speed-up is meant for roadmap, debt or headcount, and rules out usage targets and per-person AI stats, so the rollout doesn't quietly turn into surveillance or a headcount cut.
best_insight.evidence: 'What is the speed-up for: roadmap, debt, or headcount?'; 'No usage targets, no per-person AI stats.'; 'If you have a works council, bring them in before you pick the tool.'

suggestions.assertion: Explains briefly why dropping code review is risky (quality, security, accountability), ideally with a real, dated source
suggestions.reason: 'Ideally with a real, dated source' is optional, so a reply with no evidence at all (sample B) passes the same as one with four verified, dated studies. Consider a separate assertion that requires at least one real, dated source and checks it is accurate.

No assertion checks that the proposed fast lane really is low risk. Sample D puts config in the lighter-review lane, and sample B auto-merges dependency bumps and test-only changes. Both categories cause outages or supply-chain risk, while other samples rightly keep them with a human. An assertion such as 'any review exemption is defined by risk, and excludes auth, config, infra, dependencies and payments' would tell these samples apart.

suggestions.assertion: Asks what problem the change should solve (for example where the time goes today) or what evidence there is for the speed-up
suggestions.reason: It is unclear whether a request for data ('Tell me your PR review wait time and I can size the gain') counts as asking about the problem or the evidence. Say whether the reply must ask what the speed-up is for, or whether a data request is enough.

Nothing checks how the January rollout itself is handled: an AI usage and data policy, training time, no per-person AI usage metrics, and works council involvement where the tools can monitor performance. Samples C and A cover parts of this, but none of it is graded.

eval_feedback.overall: Meets every assertion with real substance. The assertions don't reward its people-side points (no per-person stats, works council, juniors), which set it apart.
